s: Part five.
Iterative refinement.

By the end of this part, you'll know how to give Claude a check it can run for itself, when to stop correcting and start fresh, how to guarantee a green test suite, and when to work one at a time versus in parallel.
Plain version.
Picture someone hanging a shelf.
If they have a spirit level, they can tell whether the shelf is straight without leaving the room.
If they don't, every adjustment ends with them calling downstairs, and waiting for you to come and look.
The shelf still goes up.
But you're now inside the loop.
And the work moves at the speed of your attention.
Most of iterative refinement is the business of handing over a spirit level.
The technical framing is this.
Claude stops when the work looks done.
Without a check it can run for itself, looks done is the only signal available.
And you become the verification loop.
Refinement converges when each iteration produces a signal Claude can read.
What manufactures that signal?
Four techniques.
One.
Concrete input and output examples.
Two.
A failing test, written first.
Three.
A screenshot to compare against.
Four.
A script that exits with a failure code.
Question one.
Practice question D3-017.
Here's the scenario.
An engineer asks Claude to write a function that normalizes invoice dates to the international standard date format, ISO 8601.
Each attempt looks finished.
But review keeps finding failures on certain inputs.
Zero three, zero four, twenty-five, written with slashes between the parts.
Four March twenty twenty-five.
And blank strings.
The engineer has become the only source of feedback.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Give input and expected-output pairs, including the ambiguous and blank cases.
And have Claude run them as tests.
Plain version: hand the person a spirit level.
Example cases with expected answers are the spirit level.
In exam terms, that does three things.
It defines done in a testable form.
It encodes the edge cases you would otherwise catch in review.
And it closes the loop.
The same move works visually.
Paste a screenshot.
Have Claude build it.
Screenshot the result.
List the differences.
Fix them.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a longer, more detailed prose description of every accepted format.
Why?
It's still nothing Claude can check for itself.
Wrong: ask Claude to review its own output carefully, and confirm it handles every case.
Why?
That's verification by assertion.
It produces a claim, not evidence.
Wrong: split the work across three parallel sessions, and keep the one that looks most robust.
Why?
It multiplies cost without adding a check.
And looks most robust is still a human judgment.
Hold on to this line.
Give Claude examples it can run as tests, or you stay stuck as the only checker.
Question two.
Practice question D3-018.
Here's the scenario.
Deep in a long session, an engineer has twice corrected Claude on the same issue.
An internal command-line tool keeps swallowing a non-zero exit code.
Both corrections produced plausible changes that didn't fix it.
And the context now holds three failed approaches.
What now?
Take a second.
The answer.
The sources give an explicit stopping rule.
After two failed corrections on the same issue, clear the context.
Start again with a better prompt.
One that states what was learned, and names a failing test.
Plain version.
If you've given someone directions twice and they're still lost, repeating them louder doesn't help.
Especially while they're still holding the two wrong maps.
Take the old maps away, and hand over one clear new one.
In exam terms, the accumulated failed approaches are part of the problem.
So anything that keeps them in the window keeps the problem.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a third, more forceful correction, listing everything that went wrong.
Why?
That's the documented anti-pattern.
Wrong: switch the same session into plan mode, to reconsider with all three attempts visible.
Why?
Plan mode doesn't remove the failed approaches from context.
They keep competing.
Wrong: raise the session's turn limit.
Why?
More turns make a non-converging loop longer, not convergent.
That last one is a cross-domain pattern, and you'll meet it in the agentic architecture chapter.
Raising a cap is not a fix for a loop that lacks a signal.
Hold on to this line.
Two failed corrections, then clear and rewrite, with a failing test in the new prompt.
Question three.
Practice question D3-019.
Here's the scenario.
A team runs Claude Code overnight, on unattended refactoring.
Several mornings in a row, the transcript ends with all tests pass.
Yet running the suite shows failures.
CLAUDE.md already says run the full test suite before finishing.
They need a guarantee that no unattended run ends while the suite is failing.
What gives them that guarantee?
Take a second.
The answer.
A Stop hook.
Plain version.
Asking the last person out to check every window is shut works most nights.
If the building must never be left with a window open, you fit an alarm that will not arm while any window is still open.
In exam terms, the notes describe a ladder for how hard a test gate holds.
Three rungs.
Lowest rung.
Ask Claude to run the check, inside one prompt.
Middle rung.
Set it as a session-long condition that an evaluator re-checks after every turn.
Top rung.
A Stop hook.
It runs when Claude tries to end its turn.
It runs your test script.
And it blocks the turn from ending while any test fails, handing Claude the failure output to act on.
Guarantee, and unattended, push you to the top rung.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: strengthen the CLAUDE.md wording with capital-letter musts.
Why?
It's still advisory.
And that's exactly the observed failure.
Wrong: require Claude to paste the final test output into its summary.
Why?
It's good practice for reviewability.
But it's still a request an unattended run can skip.
Wrong: add a PostToolUse hook that logs every test command for morning review.
Why?
Logging records what happened.
It doesn't prevent anything.
One cross-reference.
The same Stop event is used in Domain one to persist state at the end of a run.
And a single hook can do both.
Hold on to this line.
When a green test suite must be guaranteed, a Stop hook enforces it.
A sentence only requests it.
Now the rest of this task statement.
The practice questions touch it less, but the notes and exam-style items cover it.
Two topics.
First, the interview pattern.
Plain version.
Take a feature you haven't fully thought through, before any code exists.
You let the builder interview you until the hard questions are answered.
Everything gets written down.
Then you hand that write-up to a fresh builder, who never heard the debate.
In exam terms.
You start with a minimal prompt, and ask Claude to interview you in detail.
On implementation, interfaces, edge cases, and tradeoffs.
Skipping obvious questions.
When the space is covered, Claude writes a complete specification to a file.
And you start a fresh session to execute it.
The fresh session is the point.
Its context holds the spec and nothing else.
No rejected options.
A self-check in the notes describes the failure.
A colleague implements in the same session as the interview.
And the implementation drifts toward an approach that was explicitly rejected.
Why?
Because the rejected options are still sitting in the window.
Good specs do three things.
They name the files and interfaces involved.
They state what is out of scope.
And they end with a verification step.
Now the wrong turns for the interview pattern.
Wrong: write the most detailed single prompt possible.
Why?
It cannot surface decisions nobody has made yet.
Wrong: run four parallel sessions, and pick the best-looking result.
Wrong: park the feature's requirements in CLAUDE.md.
Why?
It costs context indefinitely.
And it still leaves the design undecided.
Second topic.
Sequential versus parallel.
Plain version.
When each attempt teaches you something about the next one, work one at a time.
When the pieces genuinely don't affect each other, split them up.
But only after you've proven your recipe on a couple of samples.
In exam terms.
Debugging and architecture are sequential.
Why?
Because attempt two depends on what attempt one revealed.
And an interface decision constrains the implementation.
Mechanical migrations across many independent files can be parallelized.
Two ways.
As sessions in separate worktrees, which also support a writer-and-reviewer split.
Or as a fan-out loop, calling Claude non-interactively once per file, with each run returning a short verdict, like OK or FAIL.
The rule is this.
Refine sequentially on two or three representative files first.
Then fan out.
And verify the batch with the test suite, rather than trusting the verdicts.
Reverse the order, and you get hundreds of copies of the same mistake.
An exam-style item in the notes sets nine hundred files, and a sample that dropped structured fields.
The options include three wrong turns.
Launching the full run immediately, and fixing afterwards.
Writing a path rule, so conversion happens automatically.
And running all nine hundred in one interactive session, so Claude accumulates context.
The right answer refines on the sample.
Then it fans out, with narrow tool pre-approvals.
And it verifies with tests.
This connects back to D3-015's distractor, about fanning out before the design is proven.
That's part five.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Refinement converges on a signal Claude can read.
Converge on a sample, then fan out.
Coming up in part six: integrating Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines.
